title: TWA 3
summary: TWA Flight 3 departed Las Vegas at 19:20 PST on January 16, 1942, bound for Burbank. Fifteen minutes after takeoff at 8,000 feet, the aircraft was 7 miles off course on a compass heading of 218° when it struck Potosi Mountain. The Civil Aeronautics Board determined the navigation error likely resulted from the crew inadvertently using the Boulder City departure course instead of the appropriate Las Vegas outbound course. All 22 aboard perished including actress Carole Lombard.
probable_cause: Navigation error by the captain using compass heading instead of radio navigation. The crew likely confused the Boulder City outbound course of 218° with the Las Vegas course, resulting in the aircraft being flown 7 miles off the designated airway into high terrain.

factors.evidence: the crew was not using radio navigation to follow the airway but was instead using a compass heading of 218°
the plane took off on a clear, moonless night and the airway light beacons had been turned off because of the ongoing Second World War
the crew did not realize the terrain in that direction rose to about 8500 feet while flying at 8000 feet altitude
the flight plan form was completed by the first officer but not signed by the captain, despite a company requirement to do so
the aircraft crashed into a sheer cliff on Potosi Mountain at 7770 feet elevation

events.text: Aircraft took off on a clear, moonless night from Las Vegas Airport bound for Burbank
Flying almost 7 miles off course, the aircraft was at 8000 feet approaching terrain rising to 8500 feet
Crew was using compass heading instead of radio navigation, unaware of terrain threat
Aircraft crashed into a near-vertical cliff on Potosi Mountain at 7770 feet, 32 miles southwest of Las Vegas

title: 1942 Qantas Short Empire shootdown
summary: Qantas Short Empire flying boat G-AEUH, captained by A.A. Koch, departed Darwin on 30 January 1942 bound for Kupang en route to Surabaya to evacuate refugees from the Japanese invasion of Java. At 13 nautical miles from West Timor and 400 feet altitude, seven Mitsubishi A6M Zero fighters attacked the aircraft. Koch maneuvered to evade, but the Zeros achieved multiple hits, perforating the fuselage and killing passengers. Two engines caught fire. The aircraft hit the sea at high speed nose-first, breaking the fuselage in two. Thirteen of eighteen occupants were killed.
probable_cause: Japanese military attack on a civilian transport aircraft by seven Zero fighters resulted in engine damage and structural failure necessitating a ditching; high-speed impact in rough seas was unsurvivable for most occupants.

factors.evidence: Seven Mitsubishi A6M Zero fighters fired on the aircraft when it was 13 nmi from West Timor, travelling at a height of 400 ft
Two engines caught fire from the attacks
The Zero pilots achieved several hits, perforating the fuselage
Corio hit the sea at high speed, nose first, 3 nmi from the mouth of the Noelmini River; the impact breaking the fuselage in two

events.text: G-AEUH, captained by A. A. (Aub) Koch, left Darwin at dawn, for Kupang, West Timor, en route to Surabaya
When it was 13 nmi from West Timor, travelling at a height of 400 ft, Corio was fired on by seven Mitsubishi A6M Zero fighters
The Zero pilots soon achieved several hits, perforating the fuselage and killing some passengers
Two engines caught fire and Corio hit the sea at high speed, nose first
Koch managed to swim ashore, taking three hours, and Koch, three passengers and two crew were rescued

title: 1942 KNILM Douglas DC-3 shootdown
summary: On 3 March 1942, KNILM Douglas DC-3 PK-AFV was attacked by three Japanese Mitsubishi Zero fighters near Broome, Western Australia while on approach with refugees and a package of diamonds. The pilot was wounded but managed an emergency landing on a beach; the aircraft struck water causing the right landing gear to collapse. Four occupants were killed—the flight engineer and three passengers—by machine gun fire from the attacking Zeros.
probable_cause: The aircraft was attacked by Japanese Navy fighters that were returning from the air raid on Broome, resulting in engine damage and pilot injury but successful forced landing on the beach.

factors.evidence: Three Mitsubishi Zeros led by Japanese ace Lt Zenjiro Miyano attacked the aircraft, diving and firing at its port side, scoring numerous hits
Pilot Ivan Smirnov was wounded in his arms and hip during the attack but maintained control to complete the landing
Smirnoff managed to put the aircraft into a steep spiral dive and made a wheels-down landing on the beach despite being wounded

events.text: DC-3 airborne at 1:15am from Bandung carrying eight passengers and flight engineer, transporting package of diamonds from NV de Concurrent
Aircraft nears Broome at approximately 9:00am, skirting the Kimberley coast
Three Mitsubishi Zeros returning from the first air raid on Broome sight the DC-3 at lower altitude
Japanese pilots diving at DC-3 fired at its port side, scoring numerous hits; port engine caught fire and Smirnov wounded in arms and hip
Wounded pilot Smirnov managed to put the aircraft into a steep spiral dive and maneuver toward beach for landing
Smirnoff made a wheels-down landing on the beach; right tire hit and exploded causing abrupt right turn into surf
Zeros strafed the beached aircraft; flight engineer and three passengers killed by bullets, others seriously injured

title: Crash of Halifax V9977
summary: On June 7, 1942, Handley Page Halifax V9977, being used as a flying testbed for the H2S radar by TRE, encountered an engine fire in its outboard starboard Rolls-Royce Merlin engine at 4:20 pm while flying over the Forest of Dean. The left wing broke off and the aircraft rolled over and crashed near Welsh Bicknor. All eleven crew members were killed, including inventor Alan Blumlein. Investigators determined improper engine maintenance and assembly procedures caused tappet valves to work loose, leading to engine failure.
probable_cause: Improper engine maintenance and assembly procedures caused the accident. Rolls-Royce had installed tappet valves with reduced clearance to prevent them working loose, but in field maintenance the lock nuts holding the valves in place were not properly reinstalled with correct clearance, allowing the tappet valves to work loose and causing the engine fire.

factors.evidence: outboard starboard Rolls-Royce Merlin engine caught fire
improper engine maintenance and assembly procedures; lock nuts holding valves not reinstalled correctly
fuel valves to the engines were on the wrong side of a fireproof bulkhead, as were the extinguisher bottles
left wing broke off and aircraft rolled over and crashed

events.text: Aircraft departed RAF Defford for Bristol Channel at approximately 2:50 pm on 7 June
Outboard starboard Rolls-Royce Merlin engine caught fire at 4:20 pm
Aircraft seen over the Forest of Dean with its outboard starboard engine on fire
Left wing broke off and the aircraft rolled over
Aircraft crashed in a field on the Courtfield estate in Lydbrook near Welsh Bicknor

title: 1942 Ruislip Wellington accident
summary: A Vickers Wellington bomber carrying two RAF crews and additional passengers approached RAF Northolt. During a steep turn for approach, the aircraft stalled and dived toward the ground. The Wellington crashed near South Ruislip station, killing all 15 occupants and six civilians on the ground including four children.
probable_cause: Aircraft stalled during steep turn on approach to RAF Northolt. Pilot executed an approach maneuver that exceeded the aircraft's aerodynamic limits, resulting in loss of control and impact.

factors.evidence: Wellington stalled during steep turn to approach runway at approximately 1600 hrs
Pilot turned aircraft steeply to port, exceeding safe turn parameters for approach phase
Aircraft dived toward ground after stall

events.text: Wellington approached RAF Northolt from west at 500 feet altitude with undercarriage lowered
Pilot turned aircraft steeply to port to approach east-west runway from east
Wellington stalled and dived toward ground near South Ruislip station
Wing-tip clipped main road, aircraft flipped over and burst into flames on waste ground

notes: Text describes stall and dive but limited technical detail
Conditions on Oct 18 Czechoslovak independence day contributed to number of personnel aboard
Ground impact with school children area increased casualty count significantly

title: American Airlines 28
summary: American Airlines Flight 28 was a scheduled domestic passenger flight operated by a Douglas DC-3 that crashed on October 23, 1942 in Chino Canyon near Palm Springs, California after being struck by a United States Army Air Forces Lockheed B-34 Lexington bomber. At approximately 5:15 p.m. at an altitude of approximately 9000 ft, Flight 28 was struck by the B-34. The DC-3 lost its rudder and portions of its tail. It fell from the sky in a flat spin and impacted a rocky ledge in Chino Canyon below San Jacinto Peak before crashing into the desert and exploding. All nine passengers and three crew members on board the DC-3 perished in the crash and subsequent fire.
probable_cause: Lieutenant Wilson of the B-34 misjudged the distance between the aircraft when attempting a second greeting, and when he tried to pull up the B-34's right propeller sliced through the airliner's tail.

factors.evidence: B-34 crossed over the airliner's line of flight and throttled back to allow the slower DC-3 to catch up
Wilson misjudged the distance between the aircraft
B-34's right propeller sliced through the airliner's tail
DC-3 lost its rudder and portions of its tail
The DC-3 lost its rudder and portions of its tail; It fell from the sky in a flat spin

events.text: Flight 28 departed from the Lockheed Air Terminal in Burbank California at 4:36 p.m. PDT on October 23, 1942.
At 5:02 p.m. Captain Pedley reported his position over Riverside and estimated his arrival over Indio at 5:22 p.m. at 9000 ft.
At 4:26 p.m. the B-34 bomber departed from Long Beach en route to Palm Springs and proceeded toward Riverside, circled twice near March Field, and continued toward the San Gorgonio Pass.
At approximately 5:15 p.m. at an altitude of approximately 9000 ft, Flight 28 was struck by the B-34 and its right propeller sliced through the airliner's tail.
The DC-3 lost its rudder and portions of its tail; it fell from the sky in a flat spin and impacted a rocky ledge in Chino Canyon below San Jacinto Peak before crashing into the desert and exploding.
